proposals.rationale: A critics' review chapter finds no crater matching a 12.9 ka impact, weighing against the airburst/impact hypothesis on physical-plausibility grounds.
The review finds no atmospheric-physics mechanism by which a single airburst/impact-winter effect could produce a millennium-long cooling like the YD.
Absence of consistent chondritic geochemistry undercuts interpretation of boundary geochemical anomalies as genuine extraterrestrial ejecta fallout.
Be-10 and nitrate spikes near the Pleistocene-Holocene transition are proposed as consistent with, but not conclusive proof of, ionizing radiation from a nearby supernova.
A nearby core-collapse supernova is offered as an alternative astrophysical trigger for the terminal Rancholabrean extinction pulse, distinct from bolide-impact or meltwater mechanisms.
The same ice-core radiation proxies used for the extinction-pulse argument are also floated as a possible trigger for YD cooling onset itself.

Laurentide meltwater rerouted through the Great Lakes/St. Lawrence Valley into the North Atlantic is proposed to have freshened surface waters and triggered YD cooling. Note: sourced from model-prior/general literature context (Broecker 1989) as flagged in the evidence tag.
A later review finds the expected St. Lawrence flood sediment signature largely missing, leaving the specific routing pathway (though not the underlying meltwater mechanism) unresolved.

With the St. Lawrence pathway's sediment signature missing, an Arctic/Mackenzie routing alternative remains an open, partly inferential (model-prior-informed) possibility for how meltwater reached the ocean to slow AMOC.
Summed radiocarbon probability distributions show no Paleoindian population decline at 12.9 ka, the opposite of the collapse a catastrophic impact would be expected to leave in the record.
Melt-glass and scoria-like objects formed above 2200 C at 18 YD boundary sites on four continents are presented as high-temperature evidence for cosmic airbursts at 12.9 ka.
Scoria-like carbonaceous objects at multiple YD boundary sites are interpreted as ejecta-fallout products of a cosmic airburst rather than wildfire, volcanic, or anthropogenic processes.
A synthesis of two decades of meltwater-routing, ice-sheet, and ocean-model evidence concludes Atlantic meltwater forcing of AMOC slowdown is the best-supported cause of YD cooling.
Because meltwater-driven AMOC slowdown already accounts for the YD's timing and magnitude, the review treats the extraterrestrial-impact hypothesis as an unnecessary additional cause.
The critics' co-authored review functions as an independent assessment/replication attempt of impact evidence, failing to find a crater or adequate supporting physics.
Broecker's original hypothesis frames freshening of North Atlantic surface waters via rerouted meltwater as directly weakening deep-water formation (AMOC), the proximate mechanism for YD cooling.

The supernova-ionization hypothesis is framed as a hemispheric/global-scale alternative to bolide-impact and meltwater explanations for the terminal Pleistocene extinction pulse, though evidence remains suggestive rather than conclusive.
